title: Hormuz Needs a Community, Not a Condominium
gist: Iran and Oman have outlined a temporary seven-mile transit corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, but the emerging bilateral condominium would replace the IMO traffic scheme with joint Iranian-Omani authority, with the Persian Gulf Strait Authority reportedly floating charges of up to $2 million per vessel. The argument is that this institutionalizes Iranian coercive leverage and that Hormuz instead needs an ECSC-style multilateral community including Qatar, Kuwait, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

themes.theme: The corridor deal and its limits

insights.claim: Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary seven-mile-wide transit corridor through the Strait of Hormuz with inbound traffic through Iranian territorial waters, outbound through Iranian and Omani waters, and warships excluded, framed by Tehran as an interim measure pending a permanent arrangement in 30-60 days.
insights.so_what: The first concrete mechanism for reopening the world's most important oil chokepoint; its terms define how much supply can actually flow.
insights.locator: After weeks of negotiations, Iran and Oman
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Iranian officials have been explicit that the strait will not reopen without full U.S. compliance with a June memorandum of understanding that has already lapsed, and officials on both sides describe the diplomacy as stalled with no end in sight.
insights.so_what: The Oman channel is not sufficient for reopening, so headlines about the corridor should not be traded as a bearish oil catalyst.
insights.locator: As the renewed hostilities between the United States and Iran
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Six months into the U.S.-Iran conflict, reopening the Strait of Hormuz appears further away than ever.
insights.so_what: Argues the geopolitical risk premium in crude and LNG should be treated as persistent rather than transitory.
insights.quote: Six months into the conflict, that reopening the strait seems further away than ever.
insights.locator: As the renewed hostilities between the United States and Iran
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The framework under negotiation would replace the International Maritime Organization traffic separation scheme in place since 1968 with a condominium giving Tehran and Muscat joint authority over passage.
insights.so_what: A structural change in who controls 20-plus percent of seaborne oil, with permanent implications for shipping costs and sovereignty risk.
insights.locator: The framework being negotiated would establish a condominium
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Fees would be waived for a provisional two-to-four-month phase, but the Persian Gulf Strait Authority established in May has reportedly floated charges of up to $2 million per vessel plus levies for environmental impact, cargo security and staffing.
insights.so_what: A $2 million per-transit toll would materially raise delivered crude and LNG costs and change tanker route economics.
insights.locator: Fees would be waived for a provisional
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The deal's deepest flaw is that it converts Iran's capacity for maritime interdiction from a wartime contingency into a routine administrative function funded by Arab exports.
insights.so_what: A reopening deal on these terms raises rather than lowers structural risk, so markets treating any deal as de-risking are mispricing it.
insights.quote: it would convert that capacity from a wartime contingency into a routine administrative function, funded by Arab exports
insights.locator: In other words, the arrangement would leave intact
insights.speaker: CSIS

themes.theme: Who is excluded and why it matters

insights.claim: The bilateral framework excludes regional states with the largest strategic stakes: Qatar's entire LNG business and a material share of European and Asian gas security depend on the 21-mile channel, as do Kuwaiti and Iraqi oil exports.
insights.so_what: Qatari LNG is the most concentrated single exposure to Hormuz governance, making European and Asian gas buyers second-order hostages to the deal's terms.
insights.locator: Yet the plan’s biggest flaw is not the costs
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Saudi and Emirati pipeline bypass routes carry only about a quarter of prewar Hormuz volumes and Iran has already shown overland infrastructure is vulnerable too.
insights.so_what: Caps the bypass hedge at roughly 25 percent of flows, which sets a floor under the oil risk premium regardless of pipeline capacity claims.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have pipeline bypass
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Restoring the prewar order is not an option because the IMO traffic scheme underwritten by an implicit U.S. naval guarantee and administered by nobody in particular has been shattered.
insights.so_what: Rules out the mean-reversion scenario; whatever emerges will be a new and more expensive regime.
insights.quote: administered by nobody in particular—has been shattered and hopes of reviving it are futile
insights.locator: Restoring the old order is no answer either.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The European Coal and Steel Community is the working precedent: it pooled Franco-German resource control under an institution where both sat as equals, and it functioned without trust because it was built on narrow technical cooperation run by officials whose careers depended on it.
insights.so_what: A reusable model for de-escalating any chokepoint or resource conflict: pool control, do not partition it, and make cooperation technical rather than political.
insights.quote: Neither government trusted the other, but trust was not a precondition.
insights.locator: Seeking to break the cycle, postwar European planners
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Article 43 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea already provides the legal foundation, and the Cooperative Mechanism running in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore since 2007 shows the model works with Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore levying no tolls and being paid for services rendered.
insights.so_what: Malacca is the live comparable for what Hormuz transit costs could look like under a cooperative regime: services, not tolls.
insights.locator: The legal foundation for a cooperative arrangement already exists.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: A Hormuz Community would vest authority in a governing body with equal representation for all local parties, a joint traffic authority under a rotating chair and an internationally designated secretariat so no single country could issue permits, plus a services fund disbursing against audited budgets rather than into national treasuries.
insights.so_what: The concrete design features to watch for in any announced deal; their absence signals the coercive condominium outcome instead.
insights.locator: An ECSC-type Hormuz Community would vest real authority
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Such a regime is positive-sum on paper: Iran gains a recognized coastal-state role, income and a seat alongside the Arab states, the Arab states gain co-ownership of the mechanism governing their exports, and the world gets the free, predictable, nondiscriminatory passage the Trump administration has set as its objective.
insights.so_what: Defines what a genuinely bullish resolution would look like, against which any actual agreement can be scored.
insights.locator: Tehran would gain a recognized coastal-state role
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The binding obstacle is bandwidth rather than substance: Iran resists trading a hard-won asset for abstractions, the GCC does not speak with one voice, the United States opposes any administration of the strait, and diplomacy is consumed by crisis management, so whatever emerges may merely formalize existing ad hoc mechanisms and leave conflict risk high.
insights.so_what: The realistic base case is an unstable formalized status quo, which keeps recurring escalation risk priced into energy and shipping.
insights.speaker: CSIS
